questions.question: For $x_{t+2}+a_1x_{t+1}+a_0x_t=0$ (real constants, $a_0\ne0$) whose characteristic polynomial has a repeated root $r$, why is $x_t=c_1r^t+c_2r^t$ not the general solution?
options: It is not a solution at all, since $r^t$ fails when the root is repeated.
It needs complex constants, since a repeated root behaves like a conjugate pair.
It is the general solution; only the constants must satisfy $c_1=c_2$.
It equals $(c_1+c_2)r^t$, one free constant, so a second solution $t\,r^t$ is needed.

questions.question: When the characteristic roots of $x_{t+2}+a_1x_{t+1}+a_0x_t=0$ (real constants, $a_0\ne0$) are $\rho \mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\theta}$ with $\rho>0$, $0<\theta<\pi$, the solutions are $x_t=\rho^t(c_1\cos(\theta t)+c_2\sin(\theta t))$. What do $\rho$ and $\theta$ control?
options: $\theta$ sets growth or decay, $\rho$ sets the oscillation frequency.
$\rho$ sets the starting value $x_0$, $\theta$ sets the value $x_1$.
$\rho$ sets growth or decay, $\theta$ sets the oscillation frequency.
$\rho$ and $\theta$ both set only the amplitude of the oscillation.

questions.question: Which behaviour can a solution of a homogeneous second-order equation $x_{t+2}+a_1x_{t+1}+a_0x_t=0$ (real constants, $a_0\ne0$) show that no solution of a first-order equation $x_{t+1}=ax_t$ ($a\ne0$) can show?
options: A sign alternation such as $(-2)^t$, with period $2$ in sign
An oscillation such as $\cos(\pi t/3)$, with period $6$
Geometric growth such as $3^t$, without bound

questions.question: What is the general solution of $x_{t+2}-x_{t+1}-2x_t=0$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$, with arbitrary constants $c_1,c_2$?
Find the general solution, with arbitrary real constants $c_1,c_2$, of the homogeneous equation $x_{t+2}+4x_{t+1}+4x_t=0$ for $t\ge0$.
The equation $x_{t+2}-2x_{t+1}+4x_t=0$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$, has characteristic roots $1\pm\sqrt{3}\,\mathrm{i}$. What is its general real solution?
For $x_{t+2}-7x_{t+1}+10x_t=0$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$, use the root relations to find the sum $r_1+r_2$ and the product $r_1r_2$ of the characteristic roots.
What is the constant particular solution $x^*=b/p(1)$ of $x_{t+2}+0.5\,x_{t+1}-0.2\,x_t=13$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$?
For $x_{t+2}+a_1x_{t+1}+a_0x_t=0$ (real constants, $a_0\ne0$), suppose $a_0<0$. What can be said about the characteristic roots of $p(r)=r^2+a_1r+a_0$?
options: They are nonreal conjugates, since $a_0<0$ resembles $a_1^2<4a_0$.
They are real and both negative, since their product $a_0$ is.
They are real and of opposite signs, since $r_1r_2=a_0<0$.
They form a repeated root, since $a_1^2-4a_0$ must vanish.

questions.question: Consider $x_{t+2}+a_1x_{t+1}+a_0x_t=b$ with $b\ne0$, where $1$ is a simple root of $p(r)=r^2+a_1r+a_0$ (so $p(1)=0$, $2+a_1\ne0$). Which particular solution should be used?
The equation $x_{t+2}-x_{t+1}+0.25\,x_t=0$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$, has the double root $\tfrac{1}{2}$, so $x_t=(c_1+c_2t)(\tfrac{1}{2})^t$. Do all its solutions tend to $0$ as $t\to\infty$?
options: No: the factor $t$ grows without bound, so solutions with $c_2\ne0$ diverge.
Only those with $c_2=0$; the others tend to the constant $c_2$.
No: a repeated root always produces at least one growing solution.
Yes: $t(\tfrac{1}{2})^t\to0$ as well, so every solution tends to $0$.

questions.question: The equation $x_{t+2}-4x_{t+1}+3x_t=0$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$, has characteristic roots $1$ and $3$. Which sequence is its solution with $x_0=3$ and $x_1=7$?
Because $x_{t+2}-2x_{t+1}+x_t=0$ has characteristic polynomial $(r-1)^2$, its solutions have a special shape. Which sequence solves it with starting values $x_0=2$, $x_1=5$?
For $x_{t+2}-3x_{t+1}+2x_t=4$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$, the characteristic polynomial $(r-1)(r-2)$ has the simple root $1$. Which sequence is a particular solution?
The equation $x_{t+2}-5x_{t+1}+6x_t=0$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$, has characteristic roots $2$ and $3$. Is it true that every nonzero solution satisfies $x_t/3^t\to c\ne0$, i.e. grows like $3^t$?
options: Yes: the larger root always dominates every nonzero solution.
No: every solution grows like $2^t$, the smaller root.
Yes, unless $x_0=0$, which removes the $3^t$ term.

questions.question: All solutions of $x_{t+2}+a_1x_{t+1}+a_0x_t=0$ (real constants, $a_0\ne0$) tend to $0$ if and only if both characteristic roots have modulus below $1$. Is the condition $\lvert a_0\rvert<1$ alone sufficient for this?
options: Yes: $\lvert a_0\rvert=\lvert r_1r_2\rvert<1$ forces both roots below $1$ in modulus.
Yes: it is the whole criterion, and $a_1$ does not matter.
No, and it is not even necessary, since $a_0=1.5$ can also work.

questions.question: The general solution of the homogeneous equation $x_{t+2}+a_1x_{t+1}+a_0x_t=0$ (real constants, $a_0\ne0$) contains two arbitrary constants $c_1,c_2$. Which data, prescribed with arbitrary real values, fix them and hence exactly one solution?

Consider $x_{t+2}+a_1x_{t+1}+a_0x_t=b$ with a constant $b\ne0$, $p(1)=1+a_1+a_0\ne0$, and distinct real characteristic roots $r_1,r_2$. Which formula describes all of its solutions for every such equation ($c_1,c_2$ arbitrary)?
For $x_{t+2}+a_1x_{t+1}+9x_t=0$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$, with real parameter $a_1$, for which values of $a_1$ are the characteristic roots nonreal?
